commitResults.messageBody:
Atlas handled several responsibilities in one class.

Extract them into dedicated classes to improve separation of concerns.

Atlas classes were in the default package.

Organize application, command, task, storage, and UI classes into
packages while keeping src/main/java as the source root.
Cover Atlas core behavior with automated unit tests before packaging.

commitResults.messageTitle: Implement Level-9 find command for Atlas
Add Level-10 GUI with shared AtlasSession
Add assertions to document internal invariants
commitResults.messageBody:
The codebase had no assert statements, so every assumption behind the
behaviour was implicit. A violation would surface as a wrong reply or
as an exception thrown far from the assumption that broke, which
leaves the cause hard to find.

These are assertions rather than exceptions because none of them
describe bad user input. Malformed commands keep raising
AtlasException, which Atlas reports to the user. Each assertion covers
a condition the code has already established, so a failure means a
programming error and should never reach a user.

Java disables assertions unless the JVM runs with -ea, so ordinary
runs of Atlas are unchanged. Gradle enables them for the test task,
which makes ./gradlew test the run that exercises them.

Each assertion protects the statement directly below it:

* Parser: the /by, /from and /to offsets assume the markers appear in
  order after the command prefix, which the guards above enforce. The
  substring calls that follow depend on it.
* TaskList: the constructor and add() reject null arguments, get() and
  remove() take a position the caller has already validated, and
  find() expects at least one keyword because parseKeywords rejects an
  empty search.
* Storage: save() is never handed a null list, and parseLine() only
  sees lines with content because load() skips blanks.
* AtlasSession: marking a task does not move it, so the task number
  stays valid when the reply prints the task a few lines later.

Deliberately omitted: an assertion that a marked task was previously
incomplete, because re-marking a completed task is allowed. The two
AssertionError throws on unreachable switch branches are a different
mechanism and were left as they were.

Verified with test/ui-test.sh (22 cases), ./gradlew test with
assertions enabled, and a diff of every case run with and without -ea
against the previous build. All 22 matched, so no assertion fires on
legitimate input and no behaviour changed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove duplicated logic from command handling
commitResults.messageBody:
Three commands in AtlasSession repeated the same two checks: reject a
command with a missing argument, then reject a task number that falls
outside the list. That is six nearly identical lines in each of MARK,
UNMARK and DELETE, so a change to the wording, or to the boundary,
had to be made in three places to stay consistent.

The checks now live in parseTaskNumber(), which takes the message to
show when the argument is missing. Behaviour is unchanged, because the
range error is built from the command word, which is the exact text
the three branches produced before.

The "Now you have N task(s) in the list" sentence was also built
twice, once after adding a task and once after deleting one. It moves
into speakTaskCount(), so the singular and plural handling lives in a
single place.

Parser hard-coded the separator strings next to their lengths, so
" /by " appeared twice and the number 5 appeared beside it. A marker
and its length could drift apart silently and cut a description in the
wrong place. The separators are now constants, and every offset is
derived from the length of one.

Verified with the 22 UI test cases and 22 extra edge cases covering
bare commands, out-of-range numbers, non-numeric arguments and padded
spacing. Output is identical before and after, apart from the source
line numbers in a stack trace from a pre-existing parser crash that
this change does not touch. ./gradlew test and checkstyleMain pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: TaskList: Use a stream in find()
commitResults.messageBody:
The nested loop expressed the search rule and the mechanics of
collecting matches in the same block: two loops, a conditional, and a
break that existed only to stop the same task being added twice.

The rule is "keep the tasks whose description contains at least one
keyword", which reads directly as a filter with anyMatch over the
keywords. Collecting into an ArrayList keeps the declared return type,
so AtlasSession and its ArrayList<Task> variable need no change.

Behaviour is unchanged: matches keep their original order, matching
stays case-sensitive, and the keywords are still ORed together.

Verified against the 22 UI test cases, including the single-keyword and
multi-keyword find cases, and 22 extra edge probes. ./gradlew test and
checkstyleMain pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Use a stream in save()
commitResults.messageBody:
The loop existed only to concatenate one storage line per task, which
Collectors.joining says directly and without the mutable StringBuilder.

One detail is worth stating. An empty task list must still produce an
empty file, so the trailing separator is appended only when there is
content. Writing it as a suffix in the collector would leave a lone
newline in the file for an empty list, which load() tolerates but which
is a real change to the file on disk.

load() deliberately keeps its loop. It reports the line number of a
corrupted line, which needs the index, and the stream equivalent is
IntStream.range over the line numbers, which is harder to read than the
loop it replaces. Streams are used where they clarify the code, not
everywhere they are legal.

Verified against the 22 UI test cases, comparing both the console output
and the contents of the data file against the previous build, plus 22
extra edge probes. ./gradlew test and checkstyleMain pass.

Remove duplicated logic from command handling
Use streams for task searching and saving

commitResults.messageTitle: Add continuous integration with GitHub Actions
commitResults.messageBody:
Every push now builds the project and runs the checkstyle and JUnit
checks on Linux, macOS and Windows, so a change that breaks the build
is caught without waiting for a manual run.

The workflow is the one the course prescribes for this project, used
as given: it validates the Gradle wrapper, sets up JDK 25 with JavaFX
included, and runs ./gradlew check. Building on three platforms is not
incidental. The project pulls platform-specific JavaFX dependencies,
and the task file is written with the platform line separator, so a
portability mistake would otherwise surface only on another machine.

The README now carries the workflow's status badge, which links to the
Actions tab.

Tests run headless: no test class imports JavaFX, so no display server
and no xvfb wrapper is needed.

Atlas can now keep client records alongside tasks: add a client with an
optional phone and email, list clients, find one by any part of its
details, and remove one. Client numbering is independent of task
numbering, so neither list disturbs the other.

Records share the existing data file, distinguished by a leading C
instead of T, D or E. Storage loads and saves both entity types in one
pass and returns them together, so the file still has one writer.
Optional fields are written even when empty, which keeps a client line
at a fixed field count, while loading accepts two to four fields so a
hand-written file without them still loads. Escaping is unchanged, so a
name containing a pipe or a backslash round-trips.

The unknown-word reply now lists client among the commands. That is the
only existing output that changes: the case asserting the full line is
updated here, and the case that only checks the start of that line still
passes.

Parsing keeps the offset discipline used elsewhere: every client prefix
length is derived from the command words rather than hardcoded, and the
two optional markers are accepted in either order, each value running to
the next marker or to the end of the line, never inside a marker.

Tests: new ClientTest and ClientListTest, client parsing and storage
cases added to ParserTest and StorageTest, and four new harness cases
covering add, list, find, delete, independence from tasks and
persistence across a restart. The harness expectations quote full error
messages, so the usage hints are pinned and not just their opening
words. All 26 harness cases pass, as do ./gradlew test and the
checkstyle tasks.

Tasks can now carry a priority level, so the user can mark what has
to be dealt with first.

The command is priority <number> <high|medium|low|none>. The task number
is validated before the level word, so a bad number reports the pantheon
message while a bad level reports the Fates message. none clears the
level.

A ranked task shows the level as a bracketed tag right after the status
icon, and only when a level is set, so unranked tasks keep the display
form and the storage line they had before this change. A task record
gains a trailing priority field only when the task has one, and loading
still accepts records without it, so existing data files load unchanged.

The unknown-word reply now lists priority among the commands.
